title: Kept alive by a machine
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in cardiology. Mr Fraser, 83, has been admitted after two blackouts and has complete heart block. The team recommends a permanent pacemaker.

He tells you he doesn't want one because he doesn't want to be "kept alive by a machine" when his time comes. He is alert, follows the conversation well, and lives independently with his wife.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Arrange the pacemaker anyway, as it is clearly in his best interests to have one.
options.brief: Best-interests decisions apply only to patients who lack capacity.
options.detailed: He appears to have capacity, so treating him against his wishes would be unlawful, however beneficial the treatment.

options.text: Ask his wife to persuade him to agree to the pacemaker.
options.brief: Involving family can help, but recruiting her to persuade him isn't fair.
options.detailed: He may want to discuss it with his wife, and that is reasonable. Asking her to persuade him puts pressure on him rather than supporting his decision.

options.text: Tell him he could die without one and should reconsider.
options.brief: The risk should be explained, but not as pressure to agree.
options.detailed: He needs to know the risks of declining, and they belong in your explanation. Presenting them as a reason he should change his mind, without exploring his fear, may feel like coercion and doesn't address his concern.

options.text: Ask him what he means by being kept alive by a machine.
options.brief: Understanding his fear lets you respond to it accurately.
options.detailed: His concern may be based on a misunderstanding, or on experiences with relatives. Exploring it first means the information you give will address what actually worries him.

options.text: Refer him to the psychiatry team to assess his decision.
options.brief: Unusual decisions don't, in themselves, suggest a lack of capacity.
options.detailed: There is nothing to suggest he lacks capacity. A decision others disagree with isn't a reason for a psychiatric referral.

options.text: Ask your consultant to talk him round on tomorrow's ward round.
options.brief: Senior involvement is fine, but the aim shouldn't be to talk him round.
options.detailed: Your consultant should be involved in a significant decision, but framing the aim as persuasion rather than informed choice is the problem.

options.text: Explain what a pacemaker does, including that it doesn't stop a natural death.
options.brief: Accurate information may change his view, and he needs it to decide.
options.detailed: A pacemaker treats a slow heart rhythm. It doesn't keep someone alive when they are dying of another illness. He needs this information to make an informed decision, whichever way he decides.

options.text: Accept his decision if he still declines, and agree a plan for his care.
options.brief: A capacitous patient can refuse treatment, and he still needs a plan.
options.detailed: He appears to have capacity. If he still refuses after an accurate explanation, that is his right. Agreeing a plan, including what to do if he blacks out again and offering to revisit the decision, respects his autonomy and keeps him safe.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you explore the reasons behind a refusal and give accurate information, while respecting a capable patient's right to decide.
explanation.keyDetails: He appears to have capacity. His fear may rest on a misunderstanding of what a pacemaker does. The condition is serious if untreated.
explanation.reasoning: [D] explores his concern, [G] corrects a possible misunderstanding, and [H] respects his decision while keeping him safe. The distractors override him ([A]), pressure him ([B], [C], [F]), or question his capacity without reason ([E]).
explanation.competing: [F] is close, because a senior should be involved. The problem is the aim of persuading him, rather than helping him decide.

references.title: Decision making and consent
references.note: Exploring patients' concerns and respecting their decisions.

references.title: Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 1 (the principles)
references.note: An unwise decision does not, by itself, mean a lack of capacity.
